key_insight: By internalizing execution priors as learned predictive models (inspired by World Models), agents can forecast experiment outcomes instantly and avoid many costly physical executions, breaking the traditional Generate–Execute–Feedback bottleneck.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the Execution Bottleneck: hypothesis evaluation in autonomous ML agents depends on expensive, time-consuming physical execution, limiting throughput and scalability in scientific discovery and real-world tasks.
method: Train compact world-model style execution priors that predict the outcome and metrics of proposed actions/hypotheses without running them physically.
Insert predictive reasoning into the agent loop to screen and rank hypotheses, executing only high-value or high-uncertainty candidates.
Use uncertainty-aware decision rules (predictive checks + selective real execution) to retain reliability while drastically reducing runtime cost.
impact: This approach enables faster, cheaper agent-driven experimentation and decision-making, improving iteration speed and resource efficiency for ML practitioners deploying autonomous agents in science and engineering.
visual_elements: Side-by-side flowchart: (A) Generate → Execute → Feedback vs (B) Generate → Predict (Execution Prior) → Selective Execute → Feedback
Schematic diagram of a learned world model predicting outcomes from proposed actions (inputs → latent model → predicted metrics)
Bar/line chart showing relative number of physical executions and wall-clock time before vs after adding predictive screening (conceptual, no raw numbers needed)
Icon set: speedometer (faster iteration), coin/energy meter (cost savings), shield/uncertainty gauge (selective safety via uncertainty)
paper_title: Can We Predict Before Executing Machine Learning Agents?
paper_authors: Jingsheng Zheng, Jintian Zhang, Yujie Luo, Yuren Mao, Yunjun Gao
